Alexander Shields
al-ig-ZAN-der sheelds
proper noun
From the surname Shields (dweller by the shielings or shelters); Alexander from the Greek, “defender of men.”

Biblical Definition

Alexander Shields (1660–1700) was a Covenanter minister, prisoner, and apologist whose pen defended the persecuted remnant of Scotland in the darkest years of the Killing Time. Taken and imprisoned for his adherence to the Covenanted cause, he suffered upon the Bass Rock and elsewhere, and once made a daring escape in woman’s attire, only to be recaptured, for the LORD had further use of him. His great work, A Hind Let Loose, was a vindication of the sufferings and the resistance of the Covenanters, arguing from Scripture and Reformed principle that Christ alone is King and Head of His church, that no earthly power may usurp His crown, and that the faithful are bound to maintain His cause against tyranny even unto death. After the Revolution he was reconciled to the reconstituted Kirk and at last went as a chaplain to the ill-fated Darien colony, where he died. His life preaches that the sufferings of the church are to be defended, not disowned, that the crown rights of the Redeemer are worth both prison and pen, and that the LORD raises up men to give a reasoned testimony to the truth for which others shed their blood. He counted it a sacred charge to set down in writing why the Covenanters had suffered, that their witness might not be slandered nor forgotten.

Webster 1828 Definition

Covenanter minister and apologist, author of A Hind Let Loose, who defended the persecuted remnant.

Alexander Shields (1660–1700), Scottish Covenanter minister, prisoner, and apologist.

Imprisoned on the Bass Rock and elsewhere for adherence to the Covenanted cause.

Author of A Hind Let Loose, a scriptural vindication of the Covenanters’ sufferings and resistance.

Maintained that Christ alone is King and Head of His church against every earthly usurpation.

Reconciled to the Kirk after the Revolution and died a chaplain to the Darien colony.

Key Scripture

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Col 1:18 — "And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence."

1Pe 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Psa 149:6 — "Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand;"

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the reasoned defence of Christ’s crown rights.

expand to see more

Alexander Shields is preserved because he gave the persecuted Covenanters a reasoned, scriptural testimony, contending earnestly for the faith and vindicating the cause for which his brethren bled. His labour rebukes an age content to suffer, or to be silent, without ever setting down in writing why the truth is worth suffering for.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Shields is the duty to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered, giving a ready and reasoned answer for the hope that is in us, and defending the crown rights of Christ over His church against every earthly usurper. His pen preaches that testimony must be both suffered and articulated, that the church’s witness may not be slandered nor forgotten. His imprisonment and steadfastness show faithfulness married to sound argument.

Hebrew Roots

The name joins the Covenanter cause to the duty of contending in writing for the crown rights of Christ.

expand to see more

Shields’s A Hind Let Loose roots the reasoned defence of the Covenanters’ resistance to tyranny.

His confession of Christ’s headship upholds the Reformation recovery of the church’s true King.

His imprisonment on the Bass Rock joins him to the suffering remnant of the Kirk.

His contending for the faith obeys Jude’s charge to earnestly maintain the truth delivered.

His written testimony ensured the Covenanters’ witness would not be slandered nor lost.

Usage

"A Hind Let Loose is cited as the great apology for the Covenanters’ sufferings and resistance."

"Shields is remembered as the pen that defended the persecuted remnant of the Killing Time."

"His confession of Christ’s sole headship is invoked in the defence of the church’s liberties."
